title: How Language Unfolds — and When to Check
hook: Understanding always runs ahead of talking. Knowing the rough order of language milestones — and the handful of red flags — helps you tell normal variation from a delay worth acting on.
key_points: Comprehension leads speech: babies understand far more than they can say, long before first words.
Rough markers: babbling by ~6 months; a first word or two and responding to their name by ~12 months; many words and two-word combos by age 2.
Bilingual children develop on a similar timeline — count words across both languages; learning two languages does not cause delay.
Worth a speech-language check: no babbling by ~12 months, no words by ~16–18 months, no two-word phrases by age 2, or losing skills already gained.
content_html: Language is one of the areas parents watch most closely, and a useful first principle is that understanding always runs ahead of talking. Long before a baby says a word, they're soaking up meaning — turning to their name, following your gaze, reacting to "no." The rough sequence after that: babbling strings of sounds by around six months; a first word or two, and clearly understanding simple words, by about a year; then a steady build to many words and the first two-word combinations ("more milk," "bye dada") by age two.
extra_html: Two things help keep this in perspective. First, ranges are wide, and bilingual children develop on a similar overall timeline — the trick is to count words across both languages, because learning two languages doesn't cause delay. Second, alongside the typical range there are specific signs that make a speech-language evaluation worthwhile rather than a "wait and see": no babbling by around twelve months, no words by sixteen to eighteen months, no two-word phrases by age two, or a child who loses words or skills they already had. Acting on those early — through your pediatrician or early-intervention services — tends to help most. This is general educational information; your pediatrician can screen and refer if needed.

related.title: The Toddler Language Explosion
related.hook: Somewhere in the second year, many toddlers go from a handful of words to picking up new ones almost daily — and talking with them is what fuels it.

related.title: Developmental Milestones: The Big Picture
related.hook: Development happens across several areas at once — social, language, thinking, and movement — and milestones describe what most kids do by an age, not deadlines every child must hit.

flashcards.prompt: What's generally true about understanding versus talking?

choices.text: Understanding runs ahead — children grasp far more than they can say
Talking comes first; understanding catches up later
They develop at exactly the same pace

flashcards.explanation_html: Receptive language (understanding) leads expressive language (talking). Babies comprehend many words before they can produce them.

flashcards.prompt: Does growing up bilingual cause language delay?

choices.text: No — bilingual kids hit milestones on a similar timeline; count both languages
Yes — children should learn one language at a time
Yes, and it permanently slows reading

flashcards.explanation_html: Learning two languages doesn't cause delay. Count a child's words across both languages when judging their progress.

flashcards.prompt: Which signs suggest a speech-language check is worthwhile?
flashcards.back_html: No babbling by ~12 months, no words by ~16–18 months, no two-word phrases by age 2, or losing skills already gained. Early evaluation helps.
